title: J.G. v. New York City Department of Education — ChatGPT-4 'Cross-Check' of Hourly Rates 'Utterly and Unusually Unpersuasive'; IDEA Fee Award Cut by More Than Half
pub: J.G. v. New York City Dep't of Educ., No. 23 Civ. 959 (PAE) (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 22, 2024)
author: Judge Paul A. Engelmayer

kp.k: ChatGPT rate cross-check rejected as unpersuasive
kp.d: The Cuddy Law Firm presented ChatGPT-4 feedback as a cross-check supporting its requested hourly rates, not as its predominant evidence. Judge Engelmayer rejected its use to establish reasonable compensation for lawyers with particular backgrounds performing specific work in a niche practice area. This is a finding about the submitted fee evidence, rather than a measurement of AI performance generally.
qs: In fairness, the Cuddy Law Firm does not predominantly rely on ChatGPT-4 in advocating for these billing rates.
It instead presents ChatGPT-4 as a "cross-check" supporting the problematic sources above.
It suffices to say that the Cuddy Law Firm's invocation of ChatGPT as support for its aggressive fee bid is utterly and unusually unpersuasive.

kp.k: Undisclosed inputs undermined AI-generated rate conclusions
kp.d: The court emphasized that the firm did not identify the inputs underlying ChatGPT's conclusions, establish whether they were real, or show that the tool considered relevant decisions rejecting the firm's proposed rates. The opinion does not find that ChatGPT actually fabricated inputs in this case; it identifies these unresolved evidentiary deficiencies.
qs: In claiming here that ChatGPT supports the fee award it urges, the Cuddy Law Firm does not identify the inputs on which ChatGPT relied.
It does not reveal whether any of these were similarly imaginary.
The Court therefore rejects out of hand ChatGPT's conclusions as to the appropriate billing rates here.

kp.k: Prior hallucination cases supplied cautionary authority
kp.d: Engelmayer cited Mata v. Avianca and Park v. Kim as examples of professional consequences for submitting nonexistent authority generated by ChatGPT. The opinion reports sanctions in Mata and a referral to the Second Circuit's Grievance Panel in Park. These are cited judicial incidents, not measured hallucination rates or findings that the Cuddy firm submitted fabricated cases here.
qs: In two recent cases, courts in the Second Circuit have reproved counsel for relying on ChatGPT, where ChatGPT proved unable to distinguish between real and fictitious case citations.

In Mata v. Avianca, Inc., Judge Castel sanctioned lawyers who "abandoned their responsibilities when they submitted non-existent judicial opinions with fake quotes and citations created by the artificial intelligence tool ChatGPT."

And in Park v. Kim, the Second Circuit referred an attorney to the Circuit's Grievance Panel for further investigation after finding that her brief relied on "non-existent authority" generated by ChatGPT.

kp.k: Future fee applications should omit ChatGPT absent reliability improvements
kp.d: The court advised the Cuddy Law Firm to remove ChatGPT references from future fee applications unless the tool's reliability undergoes a paradigm shift. This is a conditional recommendation directed at this firm's fee submissions, not a general prohibition on lawyers using AI.
qs: Barring a paradigm shift in the reliability of this tool, the Cuddy Law Firm is well advised to excise references to ChatGPT from future fee applications.

kp.d: The court evaluated rates against Southern District of New York special-education practice, case-specific Johnson factors, and comparable lawyers' experience. It gave little weight to broad market surveys and the Laffey Matrix because they did not provide appropriate comparators for this routine IDEA matter. It approved $400 hourly for the three senior attorneys, $250 for Erin Murray, $310 for Kevin Mendillo, $300 for four mid-level associates, and $110–$125 for paralegal work. The rejection of ChatGPT was one component of this broader evidentiary assessment.
qs: The relevant practice area is special education law, specifically IDEA litigation.
After evaluating these sources, the Court finds each problematic, and thus declines to give them substantial weight in its determination of reasonable hourly rates.
Considering the case law, along with the Johnson factors, the Court finds a rate of $400 per hour for the work of each of these three attorneys reasonable.
Accordingly, this Court finds $250 an appropriate hourly rate for Murray here.

kp.k: Overstaffing and unexplained duplication reduced compensable hours
kp.d: Separately from its AI criticism, the court reduced administrative hours by 20%, from 226.4 to 181.12, citing unexplained work, overlap, inefficiencies and relative simplicity. It imposed a 30% reduction on federal fee-litigation hours, criticizing use of seven attorneys and four paralegals for a routine application, excessive drafting time and voluminous declarations. The opinion does not attribute these staffing or efficiency problems to AI.
qs: In total, the Court reduces the hours billed for the administrative proceedings by 45.28 hours. This yields 181.12 hours, a figure the Court finds reasonable to have incurred.
At the threshold, the Cuddy Law Finn seeks recompense for the work of seven attorneys and four paralegals on the fee litigation.
A discount of the requested fee is merited, at the outset, for the inefficiencies inherent in spreading the work on this project across 11 timekeepers.

kp.k: Final reduction reflected rates, hours and settlement cutoff
kp.d: The firm sought $113,484.62 plus interest; the court awarded $53,050.13, comprising $52,386.01 in fees and $664.12 in costs, plus statutory post-judgment interest. Because compensable fees and costs through May 26, 2023 were below DOE's unaccepted $54,300 settlement offer, the court excluded later accruals under the IDEA fee cap. The reduction therefore reflects reasonable-rate and reasonable-hour determinations and a statutory cutoff, rather than a standalone sanction for using ChatGPT.
qs: On May 26, 2023, DOE offered to settle the suit for $54,300, but J.G. declined.
The Court therefore is obliged to cap the award so as not to award J.G. fees and costs that accrued after May 26, 2023.
J.G. is awarded $52,386.01 in fees and $664.12 in costs, for a total of $53,050.13, plus post-judgment interest at the applicable statutory rate.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Paul A. Engelmayer rejects ChatGPT as support for the requested hourly rates in this IDEA fee application; the firm had presented it as a supplementary cross-check.
pts.d: The opinion records the Cuddy Law Firm's position that ChatGPT-4 feedback supported its requested billing rates, while expressly noting that the firm did not predominantly rely on it. Engelmayer finds that invocation unpersuasive and rejects the tool's conclusions about appropriate rates. This is a case-specific assessment of AI-generated support for legal fee claims, not a prediction about automation, lawyer displacement, or legal-market productivity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The court relies on undisclosed inputs, uncertainty about consideration of relevant rate precedents, and two prior court incidents involving fabricated AI-generated authorities.
pts.d: Engelmayer observes that the firm did not identify the inputs underlying ChatGPT's conclusions or establish whether it considered decisions rejecting the firm's requested rates. He also invokes Mata v. Avianca and Park v. Kim as examples of judicial responses to lawyers' reliance on fabricated ChatGPT authorities. These are cited court incidents, not benchmarking results or measured hallucination rates. The opinion does not establish that ChatGPT fabricated the rate information in this case; it notes that the firm did not reveal whether the inputs were imaginary.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The February 22, 2024 opinion advises against future reliance on ChatGPT in the firm's fee applications unless its reliability changes fundamentally.
pts.d: The assessment concerns ChatGPT-4 as presented in this litigation. The forward-looking recommendation is explicitly conditional on the absence of a paradigm shift in reliability, with no date predicted for such a change. It is advice to this firm about future fee applications, rather than a categorical prohibition on all legal uses of AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected parties are the Cuddy Law Firm, its prevailing-parent client, and the NYC Department of Education in specialized IDEA fee-shifting litigation.
pts.d: The firm's AI-supported rate argument receives no weight from the court. The client receives $53,050.13 in fees and costs rather than the requested $113,484.62, with DOE responsible for the award. The opinion does not attribute the entire reduction to AI use or impose an AI-specific sanction: it separately reduces hourly rates and compensable hours and applies the statutory settlement-offer cutoff. The AI-related consequence is rejection of a purported evidentiary cross-check and advice against repeating that practice.
